sections.title: Names and Titles

video.covers: When a name or title takes two commas and when it takes none: the cross-out test, “the only one” vs “one of many,” titles of works, and the one-comma trap

written.text: Grammar 2 taught you to set off **extra information** with two commas. Names and titles are the SAT’s favourite test of that rule, because the same name can be extra in one sentence and **essential** in another. It depends on whether the words before the name already tell us exactly who or what we mean.
Two commas or no commas

When a name or title sits in the middle of a sentence, there are usually only two correct options: **a comma before and after it**, or **no commas at all**. A single comma before a name is always wrong.

items: Cross out the name or title and read the sentence without it.
If the sentence still tells you exactly who or what (there is only one), the name is **extra** → two commas.
If you now ask “which one?”, the name is **essential** → no commas.

rows: The novel’s author**,** Jamaica Kincaid**,** had only recently turned to fiction.
A novel has one author: the name is extra → **two commas**
The German physicist Wilhelm Roentgen discovered x-rays.
*Which German physicist?* There are many → **no commas**
Lisa See, author of the best-selling novel *Snow Flower and the Secret Fan*, traveled to China.
*Which novel?* The title is essential → no comma before it; the comma after it closes the phrase that began after *See*

written.text: “The only one” vs “one of many”

items: Commas around a name say: **this is the only one**. *His wife**,** Malika**,** is a doctor.* (He has one wife.)
No commas say: **one of many**. *The poet Alisher Navoi wrote in Chagatai.* (There are many poets.)
A title + name with no *the* in front (*entomologist Deborah Gordon, critic Stina Chyn, playwright August Wilson*) works like one long name: **no comma between them**.
A number can make the description complete: *two types of cells**,** OCR21 and OBR52**,** are common.* We already know there are exactly two, so the names are extra.

written.title: SAT trap: the comma before a verb
written.text: When the name is the end of the subject, nothing goes between it and the verb: ~~the playwright August Wilson, explores~~ → *the playwright August Wilson explores*. In your deck’s Fight Time, Question 10, the correct answer is D (no commas), not A.
If the answer choices differ only in commas around a name, ask one question: **could there be more than one?** Many physicists, many poets, 38 OECD members → no commas.
Ismni o‘chirib ko‘ring. Gap hali ham kimni nazarda tutayotganini aniq aytsa — ikki vergul. “Qaysi biri?” degan savol tug‘ilsa — vergul yo‘q. Ism oldidan bitta vergul hech qachon to‘g‘ri emas.
Rules after Erica Meltzer, “Commas with Names and Titles” (ch. 6), and the SATashkent Grammar 3 deck.

A.passage: During the study, researchers found that two types of ______ are very common.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: When the description includes a number (“two types of cells”), it already tells us exactly which ones, so the names are extra: two commas.
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · slide 23

A.passage: Best known for the series of 10 plays collectively referred to as “The Pittsburgh Cycle,” the ______ explores universal themes while exploring the experiences and heritage of the African American community throughout the twentieth century.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “The playwright” is not a unique description, so the name is essential: no commas, and nothing between the subject and “explores.” (Your deck’s key marks the two-comma version; the version with no commas is correct.)
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · Fight Time, Question 10

A.passage: The Austronesian language family comprises some 1,200 languages—including the ______ Javanese and Bikol, which are spoken by 100 million and 2.6 million speakers, respectively—and accounts for one-fifth of the world’s languages, making it of keen interest to linguists like Li Jen-kuei.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “The languages” needs the names to tell us which ones, so no punctuation before “Javanese and Bikol.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Boundaries #130 · real SAT question

A.passage: In 1937, Chinese American screen actor Anna May Wong, who had portrayed numerous villains and secondary characters but never a heroine, finally got a starring role in Paramount Pictures’ Daughter of Shanghai, a film that ______ “expanded the range of possibilities for Asian images on screen.”
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Critic” is not unique, so “critic Stina Chyn” takes no commas, and “claims” leads straight into the quotation that completes the clause.
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · Fight Time, Question 9

A.passage: The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) tracks comparative price list data for its thirty-eight member countries. A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: There are 38 member nations, so “member nation” alone doesn’t say which one. The name is essential: no punctuation.

A.passage: While the greater adjutant (Leptoptilos dubius) can be found in places like Dong Khanthung in Laos and Chitwan National Park in Nepal, more than 80 percent of this endangered stork species is found in Assam, India. There, wildlife ______ is on the front lines of conservation efforts to bring adjutants back from near extinction.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Wildlife biologist” is a title that doesn’t identify one person, so the name is essential: no commas.
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Boundaries #169 · real SAT question

A.passage: Long attributed to Jacques-Louis David, the preeminent Neoclassical painter of his day, the 1801 painting Marie Joséphine Charlotte du Val d’Ognes gained fresh attention in the 1990s when art historians discovered that the painting—which depicts a solitary young woman sketching—was actually the work of little-known French portrait ______ Marie-Denise Villers (1774-1821).
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “French portrait artist” doesn’t say which one, so the name is essential: no punctuation.
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Boundaries #204 · real SAT question

B.passage: In the popular imagination, ants are often depicted as brave soldiers or dutiful factory workers. According to ______ however, this portrayal is a human fiction.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
B.explanation: “Entomologist Deborah Gordon” is a title + name (no comma between them). The comma after the name ends the opening phrase before “however.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: All Non-Essential and Essential Clauses #2

B.passage: The discovery of x-rays occurred entirely by chance. In November 1895, the German ______ accidentally discovered an image created by rays emanating from a vacuum tube. Further investigation showed that the rays were capable of passing through many kinds of matter.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
B.explanation: “The German physicist” is not unique (there are many), so the name is essential: no commas.
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: All Non-Essential and Essential Clauses #6 (also on slide 6 of your deck)

C.passage: L. Leann Kanda, a researcher and sewing enthusiast, experimented with several techniques in her attempt to replicate the famous pleating of the Fortuny Delphos gown. The specific method, which the fashion ______ developed in the early twentieth century, is considered lost.
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

designers Henriette Nigrin and Mariano Fortuny y Madrazo,
designers Henriette Nigrin and Mariano Fortuny y Madrazo
designers, Henriette Nigrin and Mariano Fortuny y Madrazo,

C.passage: The editors of Home Ground: A Guide to the American Landscape turned to Arturo Longoria, a nonfiction writer, to craft the entry for “arroyo,” a term referring to the bed of an intermittently dry stream or creek. For “lek,” however, the editors chose ______ the author of The Very Rich Hours.
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
C.explanation: “Poet” doesn’t say which poet, so the name is essential: no comma before it. The comma after it opens the extra phrase “the author of…”.

C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: best-selling novel, Snow Flower and the Secret Fan
best-selling novel Snow Flower and the Secret Fan,
best-selling novel Snow Flower and the Secret Fan
best-selling novel, Snow Flower and the Secret Fan,
C.explanation: The title is essential (no comma before it); the comma after it closes the extra information “author of the best-selling novel…” that began after “See.”
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: All Non-Essential and Essential Clauses #3

sections.title: Subject–Verb Agreement

video.covers: Singular vs plural verbs, finding the real subject behind extra information, prepositional phrases, inverted sentences, there is/there are, -ing subjects, collective nouns, each/every/neither…nor, along with

written.text: A verb must agree with its subject: **singular subject → singular verb, plural subject → plural verb**. The SAT never puts the subject right next to the verb. Your job is to find the real subject.

Verbs work the opposite way from nouns: a singular verb **ends in -s** (*it makes*), a plural verb does not (*they make*). When the choices mix singular and plural verbs, the question is about agreement, not tense.
Five disguises

rows: Green tea with mint, ~~which is a popular drink in many countries,~~ **is** said to be healthy.
**Extra information**: cross out what sits between the commas or dashes
The patent ~~for the first mechanical pencils~~ **was** granted in England.
**Prepositional phrase**: the noun after *of/for/in/between* is never the subject
**Inverted sentence**: the subject comes after the verb. Ask “what were among the finds?”
There **have** been many questions about GM foods.
**There is / there are**: the subject comes after the verb (*many questions*)
Playing parlor games **was** a popular pastime.
**-ing subject or a whole clause**: always singular

written.text: Words that look plural but are singular

items: **Collective nouns**: team, company, committee, family, collection, audience → singular. *The theater company **has** traveled…*
**each, every, everyone, everything, anyone, nobody, the number of** → singular. *Each of these republics **was** established…*
**along with, as well as, in conjunction with, together with** do not add a second subject: *Orville Wright, along with his brother Wilbur, **is**…*
**A and B** → plural. *The trefoil knot and the figure-eight knot **are**…*
**Neither A nor B / either A or B** → the verb agrees with the closer subject: *Neither the algorithms nor the AI **captures**…*

written.title: SAT trap: the nearest noun
written.text: The noun right before the blank is usually a decoy. In *the average processing power of microchips—whose cores can number in the thousands—___*, the decoys are *microchips* and *thousands*; the subject is *power* (singular): **has improved**.

Fe’l oldidagi so‘zga ishonmang. Vergul/tire orasidagi qismni va “of, in, for…” bilan boshlangan iborani o‘chiring, keyin “kim/nima?” deb so‘rang. Topilgan ega birlikmi yoki ko‘plikmi — fe’l ham shunday bo‘ladi.
Rules after Erica Meltzer, “Verbs: Agreement and Tense” (ch. 8), and the SATashkent Grammar 3 deck.

sources: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar, ch. 8 “Subject-Verb Agreement”

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Green tea with mint, which is a popular drink in many Middle Eastern countries, are said to have many health benefits.
Green tea with mint, which is a popular drink in many Middle Eastern countries, is said to have many health benefits.
A.explanation: Cross out the clause between the commas: Green tea with mint… is said. The subject is singular.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Green tea with mint, which is a popular drink in many Middle Eastern countries, is said to have many health benefits.
Green tea with mint, which are a popular drink in many Middle Eastern countries, is said to have many health benefits.
A.explanation: “Which” refers to green tea with mint, one drink, so the verb inside the clause is singular too: “which is.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: A drink that is popular in many Middle Eastern countries is green tea with mint, said to have many health benefits.
A drink that is popular in many Middle Eastern countries are green tea with mint, said to have many health benefits.
A.explanation: The subject is “a drink” (singular). “That is popular in many Middle Eastern countries” only describes it.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: The black widow spider has striking red hourglass markings that makes it one of the most recognizable spiders in the United States.
The black widow spider has striking red hourglass markings that make it one of the most recognizable spiders in the United States.
A.explanation: “That” refers to the markings (plural), so the verb is plural: “make.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: The patent for the first mechanical pencils were granted to Sampson Morgan and John Hawkins in England during the early nineteenth century.
The patent for the first mechanical pencils was granted to Sampson Morgan and John Hawkins in England during the early nineteenth century.
A.explanation: The subject is “the patent” (singular). “For the first mechanical pencils” is a prepositional phrase.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Among the finds from a recent archaeological dig was earthenware knobs originally used for “pay walls,” boxes into which Elizabethan theater-goers deposited their fees.
Among the finds from a recent archaeological dig were earthenware knobs originally used for “pay walls,” boxes into which Elizabethan theater-goers deposited their fees.
A.explanation: The sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. What was among the finds? Earthenware knobs (plural), so “were.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

A.passage: The word “robot” ______ first used in the 1920 play R.U.R. by Czech author Karel Capek.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “the word” (singular), and the event is in the past: “was first used.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #14 · real SAT question

A.passage: Alicia Pérez-Porro, whose research focuses mainly on sea sponges, ______ as a biologist at the Smithsonian Institution.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: Cross out “whose research focuses mainly on sea sponges.” Alicia Pérez-Porro works: singular.
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #124 · real SAT question

A.passage: Analyst, like other dactyls that pair exclusively with one other word (e.g., “fortify” and “mortify”), ______ with “panelist” to form a closed rhyming pair.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “Analyst” (one word, singular); “like other dactyls…” is extra. “Couples.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #98 · real SAT question

A.passage: On the other hand, Newark Liberty International Airport, which ______ located in Newark, New Jersey, saw an overall increase in departing passengers over the same time period, from 16,704,844 total passengers to 23,171,827.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Which” refers to the airport (singular), and the sentence is in the present: “which is located.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #3 · real SAT question

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Radioactivity is generally not considered harmful when people are exposed to it at low levels for brief periods, but less clear is its long-term effects.
Radioactivity is generally not considered harmful when people are exposed to it at low levels for brief periods, but less clear are its long-term effects.
B.explanation: Inverted clause: the subject “its long-term effects” comes after the verb. Plural subject, plural verb: “are.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Pigeons make highly effective messengers because their speed and homing ability allow them to quickly and reliably reach familiar destinations.
Pigeons make highly effective messengers because their speed and homing ability allows them to quickly and reliably reach familiar destinations.
B.explanation: Two subjects joined by “and” (speed and homing ability) take a plural verb: “allow.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: In recent years, there have been many questions raised about the safety of genetically modified foods.
In recent years, there has been many questions raised about the safety of genetically modified foods.
B.explanation: After “there,” find the real subject: “many questions” (plural), so “there have been.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Playing parlor games such as charades were a popular pastime in the early twentieth century, before the invention of radio and television.
Playing parlor games such as charades was a popular pastime in the early twentieth century, before the invention of radio and television.
B.explanation: An -ing subject (“Playing parlor games…”) is one activity, so it is singular: “was.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: For the past several years, the theater company has traveled to various schools throughout the city in order to expose students to classic works.
For the past several years, the theater company have traveled to various schools throughout the city in order to expose students to classic works.
B.explanation: A collective noun (company, team, committee) is singular on the SAT: “has.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: When any of the committee members proposes a new regulation, the committee discusses it thoroughly and then takes a vote.
When any of the committee members propose a new regulation, the committee discusses it thoroughly and then takes a vote.
B.explanation: “Any” here means “any one,” which is singular: “proposes.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Subject-Verb Agreement

B.passage: The city of Quito in Ecuador ______ one of the rare places in the world located almost directly on the equator.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
B.explanation: “The city of Quito” is singular: “is.”
B.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #27 · real SAT question

B.passage: Tarawa, with a population of roughly 30,000 people, ______ home to an impressive 29 percent of Kiribati’s total population.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
B.explanation: Cross out “with a population of roughly 30,000 people.” Tarawa is home: singular.
B.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #71 · real SAT question

B.passage: Koumanthio Zeinab Diallo, born in 1956, is a poet and novelist from Labé, Guinea. In recent years more writers from Guinea, including Diallo, ______ to reach audiences beyond the African nation’s borders.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
B.explanation: The subject is “writers” (plural); “including Diallo” is extra. “Have begun.”

sections.title: Pronouns

video.covers: Pronoun agreement (it/they, his or her), clear antecedents, who/whom/which, where vs in which, emphatic pronouns, noun agreement

written.text: A pronoun replaces a noun, its **antecedent**. On the SAT the pronoun must **agree** with the antecedent (singular/plural, person/thing) and must point to **one clear** antecedent.

rows: The tomato is a fruit, but **it** is used as a vegetable.
Tomatoes are fruits, but **they** are used as vegetables.
he or she / his or her
Each of the researchers will present **his or her** work.
June Mathis, **who** helped… / Susan Huntington, with **whom** she…

written.text: How to answer a pronoun question

items: Find the noun the pronoun replaces. It may be in the previous sentence, or even after the pronoun (*When **they** debuted in 1983, the artworks…*).
Singular or plural? Person or thing?
If two nouns could fit (two deserts, two cities), the SAT wants the **noun itself**, not a pronoun: *the Gobi*, *information*, *that practice*.

written.text: Where, when, in which

items: **where** is only for places: *a city **where**…* (or *in which*).
For a time, use **when** or **in which**: *a period **in which** farmers were bound to the land*.
Don’t repeat the preposition: ~~in which she plays characters **in**~~.
Emphatic pronouns must match: *the quality of the writing **itself*** (not *herself*).

written.title: SAT trap: “their” for one person
written.text: In everyday English, *their* often replaces *someone* or *each student*. The SAT follows formal rules: a singular antecedent takes **it/its** or **his or her**. Also check nouns: two brothers became **bicycle sellers**, not *a bicycle seller*.
Olmosh qaysi otni almashtirayotganini toping: birlik — it/its, ko‘plik — they/their. Agar ikkita ot mos kelsa, olmosh emas, otning o‘zini tanlang.
Rules after Erica Meltzer, “Pronoun Agreement” and “Relative Pronouns” (ch. 9), and the SATashkent Grammar 3 deck.

sections.title: Possessives and Apostrophes

video.covers: Plural vs possessive, singular vs plural possession, joint vs separate possession, its/it’s, their/they’re/there, whose/who’s, your/you’re

written.text: An apostrophe shows **possession** (the dog’s bone) or a **contraction** (it’s = it is). A plain plural never takes one.
Three questions for every apostrophe

items: Does the word **own** the next word? *dogs’ collars* (yes) vs *the dogs played* (no). No ownership → no apostrophe.
One owner or several? Read the context: “each student… his or her computer” means many computers → **computers’ backgrounds**.
Does the next word own anything? In *story’s events*, *events* owns nothing, so it stays a plain plural.

written.text: Pronouns never take an apostrophe for possession

rows: *its* tail = possession; *it’s* = it is. **its’** does not exist.

written.text: Plug in the long form. *The cat plays with (its/it’s) toy* → “with **it is** toy” is wrong, so **its**.
Joint vs separate possession

items: One thing shared: apostrophe on the **last** name only. *McQuarrie and Johnston’s aesthetic* (one aesthetic).
Separate things: apostrophe on **each** name. *Cesar’s, Millie’s, and Marisol’s presentations* (three presentations).

written.text: Apostrof faqat egalik yoki qisqartma uchun. Oddiy ko‘plikka apostrof qo‘yilmaydi. its, their, whose — egalik; it’s, they’re, who’s — qisqartma.

sections.title: Modifiers

video.covers: Dangling modifiers, the noun after the comma, possessive traps, misplaced modifiers inside the sentence

written.text: A **modifier** is a phrase that describes something. The rule is simple: **put the modifier right next to the thing it describes.** The SAT tests it most often with a phrase at the start of the sentence.
Dangling modifiers
When a sentence opens with a descriptive phrase and a comma, **the noun right after the comma must be the thing described.**

rows: ~~Stretching across the city, the efficiency of Lisbon’s tram system…~~
The efficiency doesn’t stretch across the city → **wrong**
Stretching across the city, **Lisbon’s tram system** surprises tourists with its efficiency.
~~An elementary school teacher, Bessie Boehm Moore’s goal was…~~
Her *goal* wasn’t a teacher. A possessive does not fix it → **wrong**
An elementary school teacher, **Bessie Boehm Moore** had the goal of…

items: Read the opening phrase and ask: **who or what** is doing or being this?
Find that noun in the choices. The right answer starts with it.
Watch for “it’s”/“there is”/passive openings (*a website was made by…*): they push the real noun away from the comma.

written.text: Misplaced modifiers

items: Inside a sentence, a phrase attaches to the nearest noun. *…a particular food ~~such as itching or swelling~~* makes itching sound like a food.
*Which/who/where* clauses describe the noun right before them: *pesticides, which had caused a sharp decline in bird populations* (not *the environmental movement, which…*).
Adjectives go next to their noun: *inexpensive professional quality digital cameras*, not *cameras… to filmmakers that are inexpensive*.

written.title: SAT trap: the possessive
written.text: *Unlike most paintings, Chiliza’s vignette…* is right, but *Born in Antigua, Kincaid’s novel…* is wrong: a possessive (*Kincaid’s*) only describes the next noun (*novel*), so the novel would be the one born.

sections.title: Parallelism and Comparisons

video.covers: Parallel lists and pairs, word pairs (not only…but also, neither…nor, as…as), comparing like with like (that of / those of), fewer/less, many/much, few vs a few

written.text: **Parallel structure** means that items joined by *and*, *or*, or a pair of words have the **same grammatical form**. **Comparisons** must compare the same kind of thing.
Lists and pairs

rows: trapping it in webs; lassoing it with bolas; and mimicking other insects
changes in wind, runoff from sewage, and **accumulation** of fertilizers
the industry **has met** and **will continue to meet** the changes
each verb works with the subject

written.text: Look at the part of the list that is **not** underlined. It tells you which form the blank must take.
Word pairs
Compare like with like

items: ~~Ives’s music was less popular than John Philip Sousa.~~ Music is compared with a person.
Ives’s music was less popular than **that of** John Philip Sousa. (*that of* = the music of)
Plural → **those of**: *skills similar to **those of** human toddlers*. Singular → **that of**: *a level similar to **that of** toddlers*.
After *unlike* or *compared to*, the noun after the comma must be the same kind of thing: *Unlike medieval cathedrals, **the Lalibela churches** were carved…*

written.text: Quantity words

**Few vs a few** (short note): *few* means “almost none” and sounds negative (*Few students passed* = a disappointing result); *a few* means “some” and sounds positive (*A few students passed* = at least some did). Choose by the meaning of the sentence.
Ro‘yxatdagi hamma qismlar bir xil shaklda bo‘lsin. Taqqoslashda bir xil narsalarni solishtiring: musiqani musiqa bilan (that of), ko‘nikmalarni ko‘nikmalar bilan (those of).

A.explanation: The pair is “neither…nor.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Throughout the 1950s, Charles Ives’s music was far less popular among audiences in the United States than that of John Philip Sousa.
Throughout the 1950s, the music of composer Charles Ives was far less popular among audiences in the United States than John Philip Sousa.
A.explanation: Compare music with music, not music with a person. “That of” means “the music of.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

A.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess skills similar to that of human toddlers.
Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess skills similar to those of human toddlers.
Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess skills similar to human toddlers.
A.explanation: Compare skills with skills. “Skills” is plural, so “those of” (= the skills of).
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

A.passage: Compared to that of alumina glass, ______ silica glass atoms are so far apart that they are unable to re-form bonds after being separated.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: silica glass’s atomic arrangement is more dispersed, resulting in a significant disadvantage:
silica glass has a more dispersed atomic arrangement, resulting in a significant disadvantage:
silica glass is at a significant disadvantage due to its more dispersed atomic arrangement
a significant disadvantage of silica glass is that its atomic arrangement is more dispersed:
A.explanation: “That of alumina glass” means “the atomic arrangement of alumina glass,” so it must be compared with silica glass’s atomic arrangement. Only the choice that starts with “silica glass’s atomic arrangement” compares like with like.
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · Fight Time, Question 15

A.passage: In Moscow, Russia, the average temperature is 62.6 degrees Fahrenheit in June, ______ to 66.6 degrees in July, and then dips slightly to 62.6 degrees in August.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: Parallel verbs in a series: is…, rises…, and dips…. “Rises” keeps the pattern.
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #16 · real SAT question

A.passage: Without structural engineers, everything could twist and shake apart. Their know-how is vital to mastering green construction’s novel materials and innovative practices, whether used to harness the force of the wind or ______
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: capture the power that the waves have.
capture the power of the waves.
have captured the power of the waves.
capturing the power of the waves.
A.explanation: “Used to harness…or (to) capture…”: the verb forms match.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Parallel Structure #3

A.passage: The Seljuk Empire, which reigned in central Asia from around 1037 CE to 1194 CE, benefited from trade with other societies; its merchants exported cotton, silk, and fruit and ______ other valuable commodities, such as gold, silver, and agate, which were then traded locally.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Its merchants exported…and imported…”: two past-tense verbs joined by “and.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #75 · real SAT question

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess a level of understanding similar to that of human toddlers.
Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess a level of understanding similar to those of human toddlers.
Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess a level of understanding similar to human toddlers.
B.explanation: Compare a level with a level. “Level” is singular, so “that of.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Unlike a train, the length of a tram is usually limited to one or two cars, which may run either on train tracks or directly on the street.
Unlike that of a train, the length of a tram is usually limited to one or two cars, which may run either on train tracks or directly on the street.
B.explanation: Compare length with length, not a train with a length. “That of” = “the length of.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Because Antarctica is characterized by extreme temperatures and harsh living conditions, it supports fewer animal species than any other continent does.
Because Antarctica is characterized by extreme temperatures and harsh living conditions, it supports less animal species than any other continent does.
B.explanation: Species can be counted, so “fewer.” “Less” is for things you can’t count.
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Fewer vs. Less, Many vs. Much

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Despite blazing heat and constant threats from predators, many more types of animals inhabit the African savannah than inhabit other, more moderate environments.
Despite blazing heat and constant threats from predators, much more types of animals inhabit the African savannah than inhabit other, more moderate environments.
B.explanation: Types can be counted, so “many.” “Much” is for things you can’t count.
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Fewer vs. Less, Many vs. Much

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: The forestry industry has met and will continue to meet the growing changes required to stay competitive within a rapidly transforming economy.
The forestry industry has met and continue to meet the growing changes required to stay competitive within a rapidly transforming economy.
B.explanation: Each verb joined by “and” must work with the subject: the industry has met… and will continue to meet.
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Parallel Structure

B.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Even brief exposure to words associated with money seems to cause people to become more independent and less inclined to help others.
Even brief exposure to words associated with money seems to cause people to become more independent and less inclined helping others.
B.explanation: The idiom is “inclined to” + verb: “inclined to help.”
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Gerunds and Infinitives

B.passage: In recent years, the amount of time and money devoted to books by publishing companies has been reduced by both financial constraints and ______
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: the emphasis on marketing has increased.
they have increased the emphasis on marketing.
B.explanation: “Both financial constraints and an increased emphasis”: noun phrase + noun phrase.
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Parallel Structure (worked example)

B.passage: In the insect world, spiders are fearsome animals—the tiny equivalent of wolves, lions or sharks. Spiders use a wide range of strategies to capture ______ in order to avoid detection.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: prey, including trapping it in webs; lassoing it with sticky bolas; and mimicking other insects
prey, including trapping it in sticky webs; to lasso it with sticky bolas, and mimicking other insects
prey; including trapping it in webs; with sticky bolas they lasso it, and mimicking other insects
prey, including trapping it in webs, lassoing it with sticky bolas; and they mimic other insects
B.explanation: Every item is an -ing phrase (trapping, lassoing, mimicking), and the items are separated consistently with semicolons.
B.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Parallel Structure #1

B.passage: Unlike medieval European cathedrals, which were constructed largely from stone blocks transported over great distances, ______ by carving directly into solid rock where it naturally occurred, a process known as “rock-cut architecture.”
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Ethiopia contains the twelfth-century Lalibela churches, which were created
Ethiopians created their twelfth-century Lalibela churches
the construction of Ethiopia’s twelfth-century Lalibela churches was completed
Ethiopia’s twelfth-century Lalibela churches were created
B.explanation: Compare like with like: cathedrals with churches. The right choice puts “Ethiopia’s twelfth-century Lalibela churches” right after the comma.
B.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · slide 48

B.passage: The Byzantine Empire, which reigned in the Mediterranean from around 330 CE to 1453 CE, benefited from trade with other societies: its merchants exported salt, textiles, and iron and ______ other valuable commodities, such as silk, grain, and spices, which were then traded locally.
B.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
B.explanation: “Its merchants exported…and imported…”: two past-tense verbs joined by “and.”
B.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #99 · real SAT question

C.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Among pioneers of modern dance, Isadora Duncan is as renowned a dancer and choreographer than Martha Graham.
Among pioneers of modern dance, Isadora Duncan is as renowned a dancer and choreographer as Martha Graham.
C.explanation: The pair is “as…as.” Never “as…than.”
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

C.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Martha Graham was not only a great dancer and also a great choreographer.
Martha Graham was not only a great dancer but also a great choreographer.
C.explanation: The pair is “not only…but also.”
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

C.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: At 25 feet, a python named Medusa is longer as any other snake in the world.
At 25 feet, a python named Medusa is longer than any other snake in the world.
C.explanation: A comparative (longer, faster) takes “than.”
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

C.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: In the United States, neither Nikola Tesla or James Joule is as famous as Thomas Edison.
In the United States, neither Nikola Tesla nor James Joule is as famous as Thomas Edison.
C.explanation: The pair is “neither…nor.”
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

C.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Throughout the 1950s, the music of composer Charles Ives was far less popular among audiences in the United States than John Philip Sousa.
Throughout the 1950s, Charles Ives’s music was far less popular among audiences in the United States than that of John Philip Sousa.
C.explanation: Compare music with music, not music with a person. “That of” means “the music of.”
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

C.prompt: Which sentence is grammatically correct?
options: Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess skills similar to human toddlers.
Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess skills similar to that of human toddlers.
Although birds are not generally known for their intelligence, recent findings have established that parrots often possess skills similar to those of human toddlers.
C.explanation: Compare skills with skills. “Skills” is plural, so “those of” (= the skills of).
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Faulty Comparisons and Idioms

C.passage: In Tallin, Estonia, the average temperature is 57.4 degrees in June, ______ to 63 degrees in July, and then dips slightly to 60 degrees in August.
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
C.explanation: The sentence describes a series: the temperature is 57.4 in June, rises to 63 in July, and dips in August. “Rises” matches “is” and “dips.”
C.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #8 · real SAT question

C.passage: Navajo artist Sally Black’s mastery of traditional weaving techniques is apparent in her expertly crafted baskets, which typically are woven from sumac (a textured and flexible material) and ______ bold colors.
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
C.explanation: “Baskets, which typically are woven…and feature bold colors”: two present-tense verbs joined by “and.”
C.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #112 · real SAT question

C.passage: Scientists have long been uncertain whether dogs can read human emotions, but evidence is growing that canines can accurately “read” what people feel. In fact, a recent study found that dogs are able to distinguish between expressions that indicate happiness and ______
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: indicating fear and anger are others.
those in which fear or anger are indicated.
those that indicate fear or anger.
fear in anger are indicated in others.
C.explanation: “Expressions that indicate happiness and those that indicate fear or anger”: the two halves match.
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Parallel Structure #2

C.passage: Haiku poems, which contain just 17 syllables, can describe any person or object, but they are seldom complicated or difficult to understand. Each Haiku must contain a kigo, a season word that indicates what time of the year the Haiku is set. For example, blossoms would indicate ______
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: spring; snow would give the idea of winter; and fireflies would suggest summertime.
spring; snow would give the idea of winter and summertime would be suggested by fireflies.
spring snow would give the idea of winter; and fireflies suggest summertime.
spring; the idea of winter would be given by snow; and fireflies would suggest summer.
C.explanation: All three items follow one pattern: blossoms would indicate…; snow would give…; fireflies would suggest….
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Parallel Structure #4

vocabulary.note: These are the 30 words of Advanced Set 3. Every word is tested in the session check (10 per version).

words.definition: an official assignment to a particular place
words.example: The young doctor's first posting was to a rural clinic in the Fergana Valley.
Water is a recurring theme in her poems about childhood in Khorezm.
Over ten years, the small family café evolved into a popular restaurant chain.
The museum's oldest map includes a detailed depiction of a busy Silk Road market.

words.definition: a pattern made of many small pieces
words.example: Children made a colourful mosaic from broken pieces of tile for the school entrance.

words.definition: to transform into something more beautiful or elevated
words.example: Morning sunlight transfigured the grey factory roofs into sheets of shining gold.
Her designs are deeply informed by the embroidery patterns her grandmother made in Fergana.
The first test was easy, but subsequent tests became much harder.

words.definition: concerned with artistic form rather than social content
words.example: Critics called the architect's work formalist, saying it cared more about shapes than people.
The singer recorded one hit song and then faded back into obscurity.
The students formed a loose reading club that met whenever someone finished a good book.
The chef, who is of Korean descent, serves kimchi alongside plov at his Tashkent café.

words.definition: a rough patch of applied paint
words.example: The child's painting was a cheerful mess of yellow and green daubs.
The museum's kinetic sculpture turns slowly whenever the wind blows through the courtyard.

words.definition: to be a physical or living expression of an idea
words.example: For many fans, the old goalkeeper embodies the team's spirit of hard work.
Mystery is the most popular genre among readers at our local library.
Grandfather narrated the family's journey from Khiva as if it were an adventure film.
He was under the delusion that he could pass the exam without studying.
The lens produces an inverted image, so the trees appear upside down on the screen.

words.definition: the act of adapting to fit in with demands
words.example: The shorter school day was an accommodation to parents who worked early shifts.

words.definition: originating naturally in a particular place
words.example: The saxaul tree is indigenous to the deserts of Central Asia.

words.definition: to recognise or mark a difference between
words.example: Young birdwatchers learn to distinguish a sparrow from a finch by its song.

words.definition: an unbroken carrying on of something
words.example: The new bridge is a continuation of the city's long plan to reduce traffic.
The chef blended local spices with French cooking methods to create a new menu.

words.definition: to reduce to the smallest possible degree
words.example: Careful planning minimised delays when the school moved into its new building.
There was strong resistance to the plan to close the old library on weekends.
A visit to the space museum gave her the impetus to study physics.
The school added more sport lessons to counter the effects of long hours at screens.
The new curriculum includes coding lessons from the third grade onwards.

words.definition: felt or done by each side towards the other
words.example: The two neighbours built the fence together out of mutual respect and trust.

A.passage: In Los Angeles County, California, bicycle paths like the Rio Hondo bicycle path—which is about 15.6 miles long—have become an increasingly popular means of travel for commuter and recreational trips alike. Moreover, Ernesto ______ has identified bike travel as one possible way to alleviate vehicle congestion, citing the bike friendliness of the area’s temperate climate and mostly flat roads.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Hernandez-Lopez, a lawyer and cycling advocate
Hernandez-Lopez, a lawyer and a cycling advocate,
Hernandez-Lopez a lawyer and cycling advocate
Hernandez-Lopez a lawyer and cycling advocate,
A.explanation: Here the description comes after the name: “a lawyer and a cycling advocate” is extra information, so it takes a comma on both sides.
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Boundaries #153 · real SAT question

A.passage: In the popular imagination, ants are often depicted as brave soldiers or dutiful factory workers. According to ______ however, this portrayal is a human fiction.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Entomologist Deborah Gordon” is a title + name (no comma between them). The comma after the name ends the opening phrase before “however.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: All Non-Essential and Essential Clauses #2

A.passage: During the study, researchers found that two types of ______ are very common.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: When the description includes a number (“two types of cells”), it already tells us exactly which ones, so the names are extra: two commas.
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · slide 23

A.passage: The Proto-Atlantic-Congo language, common ancestor of 1,453 African languages with similar linguistic properties, ______ like all protolanguages, hypothetical: there’s no direct evidence these ancestral languages actually existed.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “the Proto-Atlantic-Congo language” (singular); the description after the comma is extra. “Is.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #145 · real SAT question

A.passage: National Heritage Areas like the Arabia Mountain National Heritage Area in Georgia ______ officially designated by the United States Congress as being “unique [and] nationally significant” for their natural, cultural, and historical attributes.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “National Heritage Areas” (plural); “like the Arabia Mountain…” is extra. Plural verb: “are.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #30 · real SAT question

A.passage: The proliferation of cutting-edge advancements in artificial intelligence, especially in its intersection with robotics, ______ a shift in the way we conceive of and interact with machines, blurring the boundaries between the organic and inorganic realms.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “the proliferation” (singular); “of cutting-edge advancements in artificial intelligence” is a prepositional phrase. Singular, active verb: “has caused.”
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · Fight Time, Question 2

A.passage: Most US states and territories have had at least one woman serve as governor. In Nebraska, for example, Governor Kay A. Orr took office on January 9, 1987. In fact, the number of states and territories that have had only male governors ______ almost every year.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “the number” (singular): “shrinks.” “Of states and territories” is a prepositional phrase.
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #77 · real SAT question

A.passage: Ann Greely of Maine had been a fierce advocate of women’s voting rights in the late 1800s. The dedication of Greely and her fellow activists ______ rewarded in 1920, when the Nineteenth Amendment to the US Constitution guaranteed American women the right to vote.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The subject is “the dedication” (singular); “of Greely and her fellow activists” is a prepositional phrase. Past event: “was rewarded.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #26 · real SAT question

A.passage: When a given industry—water and electricity are two well-known examples—carries high infrastructural start-up costs and other barriers that discourage competition, ______ of just one or two suppliers per municipality. Such industries are known as natural monopolies.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a given industry” (singular): “it often consists.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #68 · real SAT question

A.passage: The fact that many even-toed ungulates, including the Bawean deer (Axis kuhlii) and the south Andean deer (Hippocamelus bisulcus), meet the population criteria for endangered status validates the need for interventions that can prevent ______ from joining the ranks of the extinct.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The pronoun must refer to the even-toed ungulates (plural), and no possession is needed: “these animals.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #70 · real SAT question

A.passage: In the Persian language, people commonly begin a folktale with a phrase that roughly translates to “there was and there was not.” In English, beginning with the phrase “once upon a time” is common. Indeed, how a folktale begins depends largely on the language in which ______ being told.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The pronoun refers to “a folktale” (singular): “it is being told.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #157 · real SAT question

A.passage: In his pioneering work on honeybees, Jürgen Tautz uses high-speed cameras, sensory electrodes, and field observations to gain insights into the communication, navigation, and ______ who live in social communities.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Of insects” already shows the relationship, so no apostrophes: “behavior of insects.”
A.source: Your SATashkent Grammar 3 deck · Fight Time, Question 5

A.passage: Both Heinrich Böll and Camilo Jose Cela have been commended for ______ contributions to literature, perhaps most notably when the Swedish Academy awarded Böll the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1972 and Cela in 1989.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: Two writers are the antecedent, so the plural possessive “their” (no apostrophe).
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #2 · real SAT question

A.passage: Proto-Kru is a protolanguage, or a hypothesized ancestral language, of all the Kru languages (thirty-eight languages that, because ______ descendants of Proto-Kru, can provide information about the protolanguage’s structure).
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: “Because they are descendants of Proto-Kru”: the contraction “they’re.”
A.source: SAToplam Writing (@satashkent) · Form, Structure, and Sense #104 · real SAT question

A.passage: Minor inconsistencies in the data, whether on purpose or by accident, ultimately mattered little in the end, for the project was more about learning how to run the experiment than gathering accurate measurements of the ______.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: One car owns several tires, and the tires own their pressures: “car’s tires’ pressures.”
A.source: PrepPros Digital SAT Writing Course, Ch. 3 · Apostrophes Practice #6

A.passage: Guerilla films are typically made by independent producers who lack the budget to obtain permits, rent locations, and build expensive sets. In the past, these films were often poorly made; however, their quality has improved significantly. While it was once difficult for filmmakers to obtain the necessary equipment, ______
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: professional quality digital cameras are now widely available to filmmakers that are inexpensive.
now, professional quality digital cameras are widely available to filmmakers that are inexpensive.
inexpensive professional quality digital cameras are now widely available to filmmakers.
professional quality digital cameras are now widely available to filmmakers, and these are inexpensive.
A.explanation: “Inexpensive” must sit next to “cameras.” When “that are inexpensive” comes after “filmmakers,” it seems to describe the filmmakers.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Modification #6

A.passage: Environmentalists estimate that nearly a trillion plastic bags—in use since the 1970s—are produced worldwide each year. The problems that they cause are well known: unable to break down in landfills, ______ They also contain toxic dyes that contaminate water and soil. As a result, an increasing number of cities are banning their use.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: harm is caused to animals that consume them.
animals are harmed by consuming the bags.
animals are harmed when they consume the bags.
the bags harm the animals that consume them.
A.explanation: What is unable to break down in landfills? The bags, so “the bags” must follow the comma.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Modification #4

A.passage: Bioluminescence is light created by a chemical reaction produced within an organism. Most bioluminescent organisms are found in the ocean, although a few, including fireflies and certain fungi, are found on land. ______ some form of bioluminescence is produced by approximately 90% of deep-sea creatures, including fish, bacteria, and jellies.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: Saltwater habitats being dwelled in almost exclusively by them,
Bioluminescent organisms dwell almost exclusively in saltwater habitats, and
They dwell almost exclusively within saltwater habitats,
Dwelling almost exclusively in saltwater habitats,
A.explanation: An opening modifier would have to describe “some form of bioluminescence,” which doesn’t dwell anywhere. Two full clauses joined with comma + and solve the problem.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Modification #5

A.passage: Healthy marine environments result from a precise balance of factors and are therefore vulnerable to threats from a variety of sources. For example, changes in wind circulation, runoff from sewage, and ______ can all lead to the creation of ocean waters low in oxygen and inhospitable to marine life.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The first two items begin with nouns (changes, runoff), so the third must too: “accumulation.”
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Parallel Structure (worked example)

A.passage: For centuries, there have been reports of strange bright lights in the sky just before, during, or after an earthquake. Over the years, descriptions have varied widely: the lights have been described as flaring white streaks, floating orbs, and ______ Sometimes the lights appeared for just a few seconds, but other times they hovered in the sky for minutes or even hours at a time.
A.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
A.explanation: The list pattern is adjective + noun: flaring white streaks, floating orbs, flickering flames.
A.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Parallel Structure #5

A.prompt: In the 225 Advanced vocabulary set, which word means “a rough patch of applied paint”?
A.explanation: “daub” (n.) means “a rough patch of applied paint.” Example: The child's painting was a cheerful mess of yellow and green daubs.
A.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

A.prompt: What does “resistance” (n.) mean?

C.passage: For centuries, there have been reports of strange bright lights in the sky just before, during, or after an earthquake. Over the years, descriptions have varied widely: the lights have been described as flaring white streaks, floating orbs, and ______ Sometimes the lights appeared for just a few seconds, but other times they hovered in the sky for minutes or even hours at a time.
C.prompt: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
C.explanation: The list pattern is adjective + noun: flaring white streaks, floating orbs, flickering flames.
C.source: Erica Meltzer, The Complete Guide to Digital SAT Grammar · Exercise: Parallel Structure #5

C.prompt: In the 225 Advanced vocabulary set, which word means “a category of artistic work”?
C.explanation: “genre” (n.) means “a category of artistic work.” Example: Mystery is the most popular genre among readers at our local library.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: What does “mosaic” (n.) mean?
options: a pattern made of many small pieces
to recognise or mark a difference between
C.explanation: “mosaic” means “a pattern made of many small pieces.” Example: Children made a colourful mosaic from broken pieces of tile for the school entrance.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: In the 225 Advanced vocabulary set, which word means “to act against something”?
C.explanation: “counter” (v.) means “to act against something.” Example: The school added more sport lessons to counter the effects of long hours at screens.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: What does “embody” (v.) mean?
options: an official assignment to a particular place
to be a physical or living expression of an idea
C.explanation: “embody” means “to be a physical or living expression of an idea.” Example: For many fans, the old goalkeeper embodies the team's spirit of hard work.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: In the 225 Advanced vocabulary set, which word means “to reduce to the smallest possible degree”?
C.explanation: “minimise” (v.) means “to reduce to the smallest possible degree.” Example: Careful planning minimised delays when the school moved into its new building.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: What does “curriculum” (n.) mean?
options: originating naturally in a particular place
C.explanation: “curriculum” means “a course of study.” Example: The new curriculum includes coding lessons from the third grade onwards.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: In the 225 Advanced vocabulary set, which word means “an unbroken carrying on of something”?
C.explanation: “continuation” (n.) means “an unbroken carrying on of something.” Example: The new bridge is a continuation of the city's long plan to reduce traffic.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: What does “descent” (n.) mean?
options: an unbroken carrying on of something
a rough patch of applied paint
an official assignment to a particular place
C.explanation: “descent” means “family origin.” Example: The chef, who is of Korean descent, serves kimchi alongside plov at his Tashkent café.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: In the 225 Advanced vocabulary set, which word means “a driving force behind something”?
C.explanation: “impetus” (n.) means “a driving force behind something.” Example: A visit to the space museum gave her the impetus to study physics.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3

C.prompt: What does “transfigure” (v.) mean?
options: to transform into something more beautiful or elevated
C.explanation: “transfigure” means “to transform into something more beautiful or elevated.” Example: Morning sunlight transfigured the grey factory roofs into sheets of shining gold.
C.source: 225 English Through Reading · Advanced Vocabulary, Set 3
